Video footage shows Bates announcing he would deploy his Taser before shooting Harris in the back with a handgun; he was charged with second-degree manslaughter and posted $25,000 bail. Harris' family and advocates are demanding an independent investigation, arguing the 73-year-old Bates was improperly deployed in a high-risk operation and that the shooting was unjustified.

The robot managed to collect radiation data from 14 of its 18 targeted locations before TEPCO cut off its cable after it covered two-thirds of its route. The incident marks the first deployment of a probe in the damaged reactor, though high radiation levels continue to impede decommissioning efforts.

The blast occurred after a woman left a bag of explosives near a bus, which then detonated and set the vehicle on fire. His victory marks the first opposition defeat of the ruling party in the nation's democratic history. Georgia Governor Nathan Deal signed "Haleigh's Hope Act," legalizing low-THC cannabis oil to treat medication-resistant epilepsy, allowing the 5-year-old Haleigh Cox to return home from Colorado for treatment. The law creates an infrastructure for in-state access, ending the family's previous exile and marking a major shift in Georgia's medical marijuana policy. Despite the controversy, Bates asserts he completed all required training and has documentation to prove it, though officials have been unable to locate his firearms certification records. The case has sparked broader scrutiny into the Tulsa County Sheriff's Office, with the NAACP and state and federal investigators examining the treatment of minorities and the alleged forgery of training records.

In the wake of a deadly attack by Al-Shabaab militants on a Kenyan university, President Uhuru Kenyatta declared three days of national mourning. The small Islamic school where the suspected mastermind, Mohamed Mohamud, once taught has closed, with students staying home out of fear. Kenyan authorities are now on high alert, believing Mohamud, a local national, is directing cross-border attacks from Somalia while grappling with the unsettling reality that the terrorists are homegrown.

Pope Francis commemorated the 100th anniversary of the Armenian killings by using the term "genocide" indirectly, quoting his predecessor Pope John Paul II to avoid a perceived shift in church policy. By referencing John Paul's 2001 document, Francis highlighted the Vatican's prioritization of continuity over direct confrontation, especially regarding sensitive historical labels. The event, attended by Armenian President, underscored the church's delicate balance between moral rhetoric and diplomatic discretion.

Adrian Peterson will be reinstated by the NFL on Friday after a Minnesota judge vacated his suspension. The Vikings' running back, who pleaded no contest to reckless assault, must maintain counseling and avoid further policy violations to return to the team.

A Tulsa County reserve deputy, Robert Bates, mistakenly fired his service weapon instead of his Taser during the arrest of Eric Courtney Harris, who later died at a hospital. Police say Bates, a member of the violent crimes task force, believed he was using his Taser when he struck Harris, who was suspected of selling a gun and was under the influence of PCP at the time of the incident.

Chinese police arrested over 133,000 people and seized 43.3 tons of narcotics during a six-month anti-drug campaign, a significant increase from the previous year. The operation also resulted in 115,000 drug-related crimes handled and 606,000 cases of drug use addressed, though it came at a cost, with nine officers killed and 657 wounded. Jack White has announced a hiatus from touring, concluding his support for "Lazeretto" with a unique acoustic trek limited to just five U.S. states. The "first-ever" tour will feature a tight itinerary of unannounced, $3-dollar shows with a one-ticket-per-person limit at the venue. While the exact dates and locations remain vague, the run is expected to hit the remaining states he has never performed, likely including remote locations like Puerto Rico and Vermont.

CNN reports that UNICEF was granted rare access to Sanaa Airport to deliver vital aid amid Yemen's worsening humanitarian crisis. The fragile, temporary ceasefire allows for the unloading of emergency nutrition and medical supplies on the tarmac, though hostilities are likely to resume soon. More than 100,000 civilians have fled their homes, and U.N. agencies estimate 15.9 million people are in dire need of assistance.

Tomasz Lazar's photo series captures the haunting faces of Polish survivors deported to Siberia as children in the 1940s, documenting their trauma before time runs out. Through intimate portraits and interviews, Lazar preserves the stories of those who endured decades of exile, ensuring their experiences are recorded to warn future generations against repeating such atrocities.

The records show Bates completed one Taser training class and qualified 10 times with a handgun from 2009 to 2014, but the family of the man he killed claim he wasn't qualified and received preferential treatment. A naturalized U.S. citizen from Columbus was arraigned on federal charges of providing material support to terrorists and lying to the FBI. Abdirahman Sheik Mohamud, 23, allegedly traveled to Syria for training with terrorist groups and planned to return to the United States to kill U.S. soldiers and others in uniform. He was remanded into custody after prosecutors detailed his plans to attack military facilities or prisons.

Airline pilots generally have above-average ability to compartmentalize personal problems, but the co-pilot of Germanwings Flight 9525, Andreas Lubitz, had psychiatric issues that went unnoted despite a rigorous selection process. The FAA now approves certain prescribed medication for pilots, allowing them to continue flying while treating depression, though Lubitz's illness was reportedly severe enough to require injections, and his girlfriend raised concerns publicly after the tragedy.

This week's pop culture highlights include the release of a new "Star Wars" trailer, a viral math problem involving "Cheryl's birthday," and Gisele Bundchen's final runway walk. Other notable events range from a controversial ESPN reporter incident and a book on social shaming to the birth of the first quintuplets since 1969 and a literal "galaxy" recreated by Stephen Hawking and Monty Python.

Warner Bros. and director Michelle MacLaren have mutually decided to part ways on the upcoming "Wonder Woman" film due to "creative differences," just months after her was announced in November. Despite the change, Gal Gadot remains set to star as the title role and the movie is still slated for release on June 23, 2017, while Warner Bros. will now search for a new director.

More than 35 years after Etan Patz's disappearance, a New York jury is deliberving a verdict against Pedro Hernandez, who confessed to the crime but whose lawyer argues he is mentally ill and unable to discern his actions. The case has been complicated by the fact that Hernandez's confession was ruled admissible in court, while another man, Jose Antonio Ramos, was previously found liable for the boy's death in a civil lawsuit.

ABC is developing a revival of "The Muppet Show," with "Big Bang Theory" co-creator Bill Prady co-writing the pilot. The project could go straight to series if Miss Piggy signs on, as her breakup with Kermit is currently stalling production. The presentation, filming next weekend on the Disney lot in Burbank, features the original cast and early plans for celebrity cameos, though the show's future hinges on Miss Piggy's participation.

In Mumbai, a woman recounts being groped on a crowded train at age 13, an experience that has haunted her into adulthood. She highlights that sexual harassment— ranging from groping to leering— is pervasive, with 80% of women in Mumbai reporting such incidents, yet most victims stay silent due to societal normalization of the behavior.

Canadian actor Jonathan Crombie, best known for playing Gilbert Blythe in the "Anne of Green Gables" TV movies, died at age 48 from a brain hemorrhage. His co-star Megan Follows and producer Kevin Sullivan remembered him for his chemistry on screen and his dedication to bringing his roles to life.

Al-Shabaab's recent attack on Garissa University College, which left 147 dead, marks the deadliest assault in Kenya in the past year and a half. The group, now a pale shadow of its former strength, has been steadily losing ground in Somalia due to African Union forces and U.S. drone campaigns. Despite this decline, the militants continue to target "soft" civilian sites like universities and malls to protest the Kenyan military's presence in Somalia.

Former rap mogul Marion "Suge" Knight was ordered to stand trial for murder and other charges related to a deadly hit-and-run on the "Straight Outta Compton" set earlier this year. Judge Ronald Coen reduced Knight's bail to $10 million and dismissed one hit-and-run count, ruling he will face one count of murder, attempted murder, and one count of hit-and-run. Knight, who faces up to life in prison if convicted, was seen smiling to his fiancée as he was led out of court in handcuffs.

National Park Week, running from April 18 to 26, will offer free admission to the 128 U.S. national parks that typically charge fees, including iconic sites like Yosemite and Yellowstone. The initiative, hosted by the National Park Service and the National Park Foundation, encourages visitors to explore through events like astronomy parties and Junior Ranger activities, with more details available on FindYourPark.com and NationalParkWeek.org.

The U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development reports that 7.7 million low-income households spend over half of their income on rent, forcing hard choices between housing and essential needs. Additionally, the agency warns that the nation is on track to lose over 125,000 affordable housing units by 2020 due to expiring rent controls, prompting HUD to launch preservation efforts and the Rental Assistance Demonstration initiative to attract private investment and repair public housing.

An American citizen was shot multiple times while driving in Karachi, Pakistan, and is currently unconscious but expected to survive. The attack occurred as she was picking up her daughters from school, and assailants threw pamphlets stating "America should be burnt." U.S. officials are closely monitoring the investigation, and the victim, who has lived in Pakistan since 1996, is being treated at a local hospital.

A jury of Rolling Stone's peers has condemned the magazine's discredited "A Rape on Campus" story as journalistic malpractice. The report, which detailed a gang rape at a University of Virginia fraternity, was pulled after it unraveled under scrutiny, revealing that the author never verified her sources or confronted attackers. Despite the magazine's refusal to fire staff or restructure its newsroom, the fallout has sparked a nationwide debate about campus sexual violence.

Jon Cryer reprised his iconic record-store dance to "Try a Little Tenderness" on "The Late Late Show," dancing alongside James Corden to fulfill a "childhood dream." The recreation celebrated the 1986 film classic, delighting fans who have grown alongside the "Pretty in Like" star over the decades.

Public outrage over "religious freedom" bills in Arkansas and Indiana caught governors off guard, despite their awareness that most Americans oppose such discrimination. Businesses, al alarmed by potential boycotts, have pressbacked the laws, recognizing that support for anti-gay bias threatens their bottom line, especially as LGBT travelers represent a rapidly growing market segment.

Ines Dumig's photo series "Apart Together" follows Somali refugee Sahra, who fled her home at 14 and now lives in Germany under "suspension of deportation." Dumig was drawn to Sahra's resilience and her ability to reflect on her experiences, aiming to universalize her story to highlight the shared human experience of feeling "strong" or "lost." The project serves as both a documentation of Sahra's journey and a broader reflection on isolation, identity, and the search for dignity amid bureaucratic indifference.

Jarret Stoll of the L.A. Kings was arrested at a Las Vegas resort pool on charges of possession of controlled substances, including cocaine and ecstasy. He was released on $5,000 bail as the Kings launched an internal investigation into the incident. The 32-year-old center, who has been with the team since 2008, was not with the Kings during their playoff absence this season.

Police initially believed a shoplifter's gun was locked and unloaded, but 10 seconds later, Mario Valencia fired a shot into the air. An officer then deliberately drove a patrol car into him to stop the threat, an tactic justified by the chief despite the gun lock being engaged. Valencia was hospitalized and jailed on 15 charges after leading police on a chase from Tucson to a Marana Walmart.

Two Delaware boys remain comacent in a Philadelphia hospital two weeks after their family fell ill during a U.S. Virgin Islands trip, likely due to pesticide exposure. Their father is conscious but paralyzed, while the mother has been released to occupational therapy. The EPA found methyl bromide in their rental villa, which is under investigation as the cause of their severe conditions.

A suicide car bomb attack near the U.S. Consulate in Irbil was claimed by ISIS, killing at least four people and injiting 18. All U.S. Consulate personnel were safe, and the State Department is investigating the bombing with the Kurdish government.

More than 300 suspects have been arrested in South Africa following deadly attacks on foreigners that killed at least five people and forced thousands to flee. The government condemned the violence, emphasizing that frustration cannot justify the attacks, while police and charities worked to provide refuge and stop further bloodshed. The unrest stems from economic and social tensions, but the government urged citizens to remember the country's history of seeking refuge from African neighbors.

After spending his entire life in foster care, 16-year-old Davion Navar Henry Only finally was adopted by Connie Going and her family in Ohio, ending his years of hoping for a "forever parent." The adoption was finalized on April 22, with Only expressing that he now officially gets to call Going "mom" for real.

Democrats are increasingly focusing on economic inequality as a central campaign issue, but their efforts are constrained by a campaign finance system that necessitates courting Wall Street donors. With potential nominees like Hillary Clinton and Martin O'Malley emphasizing the wealth gap, the path to a "leftward" party is complicated by figures like Chuck Schumer and President Obama, who have relied on financial industry support to win elections despite a dwing traditional labor base.

Saudi Arabia has launched over 1,200 airstrikes in Yemen to target Houthi rebels, whom they accuse of being Iranian-backed and threatening regional stability. The campaign, now in its third week, has failed to drive the rebels back, instead prompting a growing humanitarian crisis with rising civilian casualties and mass displacement. The U.N. Security Council recently imposed an arms embargo on the Houthis and their allies, aiming to curb the violence and regional proxy war between Saudi Arabia and Iran.

Joy Womack, an American principal ballerina at the Kremlin Ballet Theatre, struggles financially despite her prestigious position. Having left the Bolshoi Ballet Academy in 2013 amid controversy, Womack now earns roughly $240 a month, a sum that has diminished due to the weakening ruble. She relies on a friend for housing and takes extra performances abroad to make ends meet, noting that "for anyone paid a salary in rubles, especially since the crisis, it is extremely difficult."

Six Minnesota men were arrested for conspiring to join ISIS by traveling to Syria, having plotted for 10 months and recruiting each other through peer-to-peer influence. The group, ranging from 19 to 21 years old, was intercepted before departure, with some arrested in Minneapolis and San Diego after attempting to cross into Mexico.

Sierra Sharry and Lane Smith were about to become parents in July. Sharry was eight months pregnant when Smith fell and hit his head. He was taken to the OU Medical Center in Oklahoma City, but he never recovered. On July 13th, 2014, Sharry posted on Facebook that she had lost her best friend and the father of her unborn child. Their son, Taos, arrived a few weeks later. When it was time for his six-month pictures, Sharry had a special request. She asked the photographer to make their family complete, just for one picture.

By now, you probably have an opinion on the controversy over Indiana's religious freedom law. Some people support the growing number of companies criticizing the law, saying it allows businesses to discriminate against gays and lesbians. Others, like Indiana Gov. Mike Pence, are surprised by the backlash and say the law is similar to a federal law and laws in 19 other states. The issue is divisive because the debate over religious freedom and gay rights is often heated, and because people can interpret the motives behind the law differently.

Fans of Lucille Ball want her statue removed from a park in Celoron, New York. They say the bronze statue, which shows her holding a bottle of Vitameatavegamin, looks ugly and does not look like her. The mayor and other people have also said they do not like the statue. Even though the statue has looked unflattering since 2009, it has still drawn tourists to the comedian's birthplace for pictures.

First, this was the first time in Nigeria's history that the opposition party defeated the ruling party in democratic elections. The previous time Buhari came to power was by force, but this time he won by the ballot box.

Buhari defeated the incumbent, Goodluck Jonathan, by about two million votes.

CNN reports that Iranians celebrated in the streets and online after a deal with the United States and other world powers ended years of sanctions. Young people waved flags from their cars, blasted music, and chused the hashtag #IranTalks. On Thursday night, Tehran's Vali Asr street turned into a party with car horns blaring, men dancing in traffic, and people waving U.S. dollar bills.

A fourth man has been added to a legal case involving a plot to support terrorists and help them join ISIS. The new man, Dilkhayot Kasimov, joins three other men who were already charged. The three original men are Abdurasul Hasanovich Juraboev, Akhror Saidakhmetov, and Abror Habibov. They are charged with giving support to a foreign terrorist group. They have pleaded not guilty. It is not clear if the new man, Kasimov, has been arrested.

A third "blood moon" appeared in a series of four eclipses early Saturday morning. The moon turned fully dark at 4:58 a.m. Pacific Time (7:58 a.m. ET). It stayed in Earth's shadow for nearly five minutes, which NASA says is the shortest total eclipse of the century. During the eclipse, the moon turned a burnt-orange color, giving it the nickname "blood moon."

Istanbul, Turkey (CNN) -- On Tuesday, many Turks were confused and scared by a major power outage. An elderly woman with a headscarf asked why she couldn't enter the subway. She was one of millions left wondering what was happening. Across Turkey, dozens of cities lost power for hours. Millions of people were affected, including those stuck on stopped trains and subways.

California's Governor Jerry Brown has ordered mandatory water cuts for residents, businesses, and farms. The state wants cities and towns to reduce water use by 25% because of a severe drought. Brown said, "The idea of having a nice green lawn watered every day is going to be a thing of the past."

The 25% cut in water use will save about 1.5 million acre-feet of water over the next nine months. One acre-foot of water is about 325,000 gallons.

Two years ago, Mike Premeau and Kathy Danke started a small business called Memories Gourmet Pizza Co. in Wisconsin. They were successful in getting their frozen pizzas, including breakfast and gluten-free options, into stores in Nichols, west of Green Bay. They built a loyal customer base. However, this week, people began mistaking them for Memories Pizza of Walkerton, Indiana. That business made national news after its owners said they would refuse to cater a same-sex wedding. People posted angry comments on Memories Gourmet Pizza's Facebook page and called its phone number to protest.

A team of archaeologists from the University of Veterinary Medicine Vienna found a complete camel skeleton under a cellar in Tull, Austria. They had discovered the bones while digging at a shopping center construction site between 2006 and 2007.

At first, the researchers thought the bones belonged to a large horse or cow. However, looking at the neck bones, jaw, and foot bones, they realized it was a camel.

Andrew Getty, a 47-year-old grandson of J. Paul Getty, died Tuesday afternoon at his home in Los Angeles. His parents, Ann and Gordon Getty, asked the media to respect their privacy during this difficult time.

The Los Angeles County coroner said the death appears to be natural causes or an accident. Investigators found some medication at the scene, but they do not know if Andrew was taking it or what his medical history was.

A German pilot named Andreas Lubitz crashed a plane into the French Alps on March 24, killing everyone on board. The latest report says he sped up the plane's descent. It is terrifying to try to understand what drove him to do this.

As the investigation unfolds, we will learn more about how much Lubitz kept his mental illness secret, or how much help he sought. His battle with depression raises important questions. Should he have walked away from his job? Should his doctors have sounded alarm bells?

His case raises larger and important issues about people who are burdened with mental illness and the pressure of its stigma.

April 8, 2015. After a report about the U.S. and Cuba, CNN Student News talks about California's historic drought. Its effects might spread across the nation. There is a flu outbreak in Chicago, but it does not infect people. A proposed tunnel would connect Denmark and Germany with an undersea road and rail line. A man named Kamron Taylor escaped from jail in Illinois on Wednesday. He attacked a guard, stole his uniform and SUV, and fled. Authorities searched for him until Friday night, when Chicago police spotted him. The guard described Taylor, and police arrested him. Taylor had a neck tattoo of the name "Gertrude," which helped officials identify him.

Prince Harry is going to Australia for four weeks. He is 30 years old and is ending his military career. He will work and live with the Australian Army in Sydney, Darwin, and Perth. He has spent time with Australian troops many times during his 10-year career.

Three people have been charged with planning to kill a former Florida inmate.

The men are Thomas Jordan Driver, 25; David Elliot Moran, 47; and Charles Thomas Newcomb, 42. Two of them are former Florida corrections officers, and one was a trainee.

The plot started after an FBI informant joined a Ku Klux Klan group. The men discussed wanting the former inmate to be "six feet under," which means dead.

The former inmate was about to be released from prison at the time.

Lewes, Switzerland (CNN) -- A series of talks wrapped up Thursday in Lausanne as a group of world powers known as the P5+1 reached a framework agreement with Iran over the country's nuclear program. The success of that agreement remains to be seen. The parties have until the end of June to work out the details and put the plan to paper. But the talks this week were, nevertheless, historic, particularly for the otherwise frozen U.S.-Iranian relationship. But that's not to say they were glamorous. In fact, the negotiations this week provided a modern demonstration of diplomacy at its best, but also at its most hectic.

A bomb exploded near a United Nations vehicle in the town of Garowe in Somalia on Monday morning. The explosion killed six people, including four workers from the UNICEF children's aid agency. Somalia's President called the attack "an attack against the future of our country." The blast happened about 8 a.m. in the capital of the Puntland region. The attack followed another incident on Sunday in which three African Union troops died in an ambush in the Lower Shabelle region. The Al-Shabaab terrorist group claimed responsibility for the Monday attack.

Prince Harry arrived in Australia on Monday. The 30-year-old royal will spend four weeks with the country's military. Before starting his duty, he visited the Australian War Memorial in the capital, Canberra. He paid his respects at the Tomb of the Unknown Australian Soldier. A crowd of onlookers gathered to watch him. Some took photos, while a young boy held a sign that said, "Red Heads Rule!" The Australian Defence Forces said last week that Harry "will work and live alongside colleagues in the Australian Army in a number of regiments in Sydney, Darwin and Perth."

Australia, a close friend of the United States, has agreed to share some information with Iran. Australian Foreign Minister Julie Bishop said the deal is "an informal arrangement" meant to track Australians traveling to Iraq to fight for ISIS. However, one Australian lawmaker called the move "dancing with the devil." Over the weekend, Bishop became the first Australian government minister to visit Iran in 12 years, meeting with President Hassan Rouhani. The intelligence-sharing deal was announced in an interview released Monday that Bishop gave to the Australian Broadcasting Corporation while in Tehran.

Maccary, France (CNN) Tests on the flight data recorder found from the downed Germanwings Flight 9525 show that co-pilot Andreas Lubitz purposely used the controls to speed up the plane's descent, according to the French air accident investigation agency, the BEA. The flight data recorder, or "black box," was found Thursday by recovery teams that have spent days since the March 24 crash scouring the mountainside in the French Alps where the plane went down. A statement from the BEA on Friday said its teams had immediately begun to investigate its contents.

A group called Sea Shepherd chased a ship named the Thunder for 110 days, from Antarctica to the coast of west Africa. They caught the ship after it sent a distress call. Sea Shepherd had been following the Thunder, which Interpol had put on a "purple notice" for suspected fraud and fisheries-related crimes.

Most days, 16-year-old Jason Zobott walks into Huntley High School in suburban Chicago around 7:30 a.m. like any high schooler might. It's what he does the rest of the day that's not so typical. Zobott is enrolled in Huntley High's blended learning program, which mixes online classes with traditional classroom learning. One-third of the school's 2,700 students are enrolled. In 2015, the school is working toward enrolling the majority of its students. "Having to work online makes it really accessible to do the work that I have to get done," said Zobott, a top-ranked junior who balances a heavy load of extracurricular activities with schoolwork. Days after a terrible attack in Garissa, Kenya carried out air strikes against the group Al-Shabaab in Somalia. A military officer said the attacks were not revenge for the massacre at Garissa University College that killed almost 150 people. The officer said, "Attacks on Al-Shabaab bases started in 2011 and are still happening. This is not revenge for the Garissa attack. The operation has been ongoing." It is normal for Kenyan military officers not to give their names to the media.

Pope Francis gave a traditional Easter speech. He reminded people that the Vatican is a country and he is a moral leader. He talked about the suffering in places like Iraq and Syria. He asked for an end to all violence. He specifically asked for no more bloodshed in those countries and for help to get to people who need it. He told the world not to ignore the tragedy and the refugees.

Students and teachers at Duke University marched on Wednesday afternoon. They were chanting because a noose was found hanging from a tree on campus.

The rope noose was found near a student center at 2 a.m. Duke officials are asking anyone with information to call campus police.

Photos of the noose were shared on social media, causing outrage. At a forum held near where the noose was hung, hundreds of people gathered. They said, "This is no Duke we will accept. This is no Duke we want. This is not the Duke we're here to experience."

A U.S. citizen named Muhanad Mahmoud Al Farekh was flown back from Pakistan to the United States. He is 29 years old. He is accused of planning to help terrorists. He was supposed to enter a plea in court on Thursday, but he did not. The charges say he agreed to give help to al Qaeda.

A border guard was killed in a shootout with militants in Yemen this week, the Saudi Press Agency reported Thursday. This is the first publicly known death since Saudi Arabia began airstrikes against rebels in its southern neighbor.

The clash happened Wednesday night at the border in southwestern Saudi Arabia's Asir region. Militants on the Yemeni side opened fire on Saudi border troops, who returned the fire.

Besides the slain border guard -- identified as Cpl. Salman Ali Yahya al-Maliki -- 10 others suffered injuries that were not life-threatening, the Saudi media outlet said.

I went to the Al Marmoum camel race in Dubai with some nervousness. As the only Gulf national working for CNN, I was expected to know about camel racing, which is an old tradition in the area. But even though I tried to wear a kandora, the national dress of the UAE, my modern way of life makes me a total outsider in this world.

A happy farm owner took us inside the majlis, which is the meeting area where the camel owners are gathering. The big space of the majlis felt like an ornate theater. The camel owners were sitting on the floor, eating a'aish, a traditional Arabic dish of fish and rice, laid out in front of them. The conversation was loud and exciting.

Havana, Cuba (CNN)Charlie Hill, 65, has lived in Cuba for 43 years to avoid charges of killing a New Mexico police officer and hijacking a plane to Havana. After two years trying to reach him, CNN sat down with Hill. He says he is thinking about leaving Cuba for the first time to return to the United States.

On April 3, 2015, CNN Student News covered international headlines from Switzerland, Kenya, and the Pacific Ocean. The segment focused on California's historic drought and the water usage restrictions affecting residents and businesses. It also mentioned two religious holidays being celebrated worldwide and looked at topics related to U.S. National Parks. The episode also included a transcript and a "Roll Call" request feature.

CNN reports that Misao Okawa, the world's oldest person, has died at age 117. She passed away on Wednesday morning in Osaka, Japan. Okawa was born on March 5, 1898. She is survived by three children, four grandchildren, and six great-grandchildren. Her family ran a kimono shop in Osaka. A worker at the nursing home where she lived since 1997 described her as a person with a mild character who loved to eat. Her favorite food was sushi and udon noodles. She ate a lot of cake for her birthday last March 5.

As the Missouri National Guard got ready to go to Ferguson to stop riots that happened last year, the guard used strong words like "enemy forces" and "adversaries" to talk about protesters, according to documents gotten by CNN. The guard went to Ferguson to help police officers, whom many community leaders and civil rights activists accused of using too much force and making a bad situation in protests that happened sporadically from August through the end of the year.

Gunmen attacked the education ministry in Mogadishu, Somalia, on Tuesday. A suicide car bombing happened first, and then the gunmen went inside. At least 12 people were killed and 16 were hurt. The group Al-Shabaab took responsibility for the attack. Five gunmen went into the two-story building and shot people inside.

Gregory Margolin is 87 years old. He was a 16-year-old Jewish recruit who fought in the Soviet Red Army during World War II. He fought the Nazis while his family fled. He did not tell people he was Jewish because many people were being killed. This year, in Ukraine, he found himself surrounded by war again. Margolin was a sniper who rose to be a commander in the army. His old uniform is still adorned with medals from his time in the military. His granddaughter Liora still marvels at his stories from the war. She is amazed that he managed to survive.

More than 200 Nigerian schoolgirls disappeared over a year ago. They were taken from their school in Chibok, Nigeria, exactly 365 days ago. The girls are still missing. Many people feel the government and the world have failed to help find them. This event reminds people that young girls can be hurt by bad people, and the world often forgets these sad stories.

In Norway, radio is changing. The country is getting rid of the old FM system. By next year, FM radio will be completely gone. This is the first time a whole country has done this.

Even though FM is gone, radio will not stop. People will just use digital radio instead. The government in Oslo says many people have already switched. On the old FM system, there are only five stations. On the new digital system, there are four times that many, about twenty stations. Half the country already listens to digital radio, said the Culture Minister.

Everyone loves a great comeback story, especially one that is big enough to fill a whole room. After being removed from science books for over a century, a new study suggests the Brontosaurus belongs to its own group and deserves its own name. O.C. Marsh first named the Brontosaurus in 1879 after he received 25 crates of bones discovered at Como Bluff, Wyoming, according to the Yale Peabody Museum of Natural History. Similar to, though not as large as the Apatosaurus discovered a couple of years prior, Marsh named the dinosaur "Brontosaurus," or "thunder lizard."

CNN reports that Al Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula (AQAP) is offering a reward of 20 kilograms of gold—worth about $774,000—to anyone who kills or captures two specific men. The targets are Abdelmalik Badruddin Al-Houthi, the leader of the rebels who took Yemen's capital, and former Yemeni President Ali Abdullah Saleh. AQAP calls these men the "two heads of evil." This offer comes as part of a complex battle involving many different groups fighting for control of Yemen.

Before landing a gyrocopter on the Capitol lawn Wednesday, Doug Hughes wrote about his intentions and the reasons behind them on a website called thedemocracyclub.org. The 61-year-old Florida postal carrier wrote in an online post titled "Your Pilot" that the point of the flight was to spotlight corruption in DC and, more importantly, to present the solution(s) to the institutional graft. "My flight is not a secret," the post says. Before he took off, he sent an Email to info@barackobama.com. The letter was intended to persuade the guardians of the Capitol that he is not a threat and that shooting him down will be a bigger headache than letting him deliver these letters to Congress.

Bad news for Rio de Janeiro before the 2016 Olympics: many dead fish were found in the Rodrigo de Freitas lagoon. With just over a year until the Games start, officials from the legislative assembly of Rio de Janeiro started an investigation on Monday to find why the fish died. The group will work with the State Environmental Institute and the Secretariat of State for the Environment.

Anthony Ray Hinton is 58 years old. He spent nearly 30 years on Alabama's death row. Until one week ago, his murder convictions were wiped clean, and Hinton walked out of a county jail in Birmingham. "I have to pinch myself to tell myself that I'm free," he told CNN's Brooke Baldwin on Friday. "It's going to take a little time, but I'll get used to it." Hinton had to get used to much worse. For 30 years, he spent most of his time locked in a 5-by-7 cell.

CNN reports that a poll about the UK election debate between seven party leaders found no clear winner.

The pollsters had different results. Comres for ITV gave David Cameron, Ed Miliband, and Nigel Farage tied first place with 21% each, while Nicola Sturgeon came close behind with 20%. A separate poll by ICM for The Guardian gave Ed Miliband 25%, David Cameron 24%, Nigel Farage 19%, and Nicola Sturgeon 17%.

A New York judge has ruled that Facebook is an acceptable way to serve divorce papers. Ellanora Arthur Baidoo has been trying to divorce her husband for several years, but her lawyer says they cannot find Victor Sena Blood-Dzraku to give him the papers. Baidoo has reached her husband by phone, and he has told her he has no fixed address and no place of employment.

It sounds like a science fiction movie. A person has a terrible accident and ends up in the hospital, brain-dead and on life support. Doctors ask the family about organ donation. Usually, this saves up to eight lives. But in this case, the family is asked to donate the whole body to save just one person. Maybe a quadriplegic with a working mind but a failing body. Although this sounds crazy, Italian physician Dr. Sergio Canavero says we are nearing "HEAVEN" (an acronym for head anastomosis venture; anastomosis is surgically connecting two parts).

In 2013, an Atlanta hospital rejected Anthony Stokes for a heart transplant because of his "history of non-compliance." Two years later, Stokes died after leading police on a high-speed chase. The chase started when he carjacked someone, burglarized a home, and shot at an elderly woman.

The sun had not risen over Garissa University College. Most students were still sleeping. A few had woken up to attend early morning Christian prayers. Suddenly, the attack began. It started with an explosion and gunshots around 5:30 a.m. Thursday (10:30 p.m. ET Wednesday) at the Kenyan school's front gates. The attackers continued to fire as they moved through the campus. The Red Cross said they stopped at a girls' dormitory. At one point, they burst into a room where Christians had gathered and took hostages, said lecturer Joel Ayora.

A white casket sat at the front of New Shiloh Baptist Church in West Baltimore. A gospel choir sang for a large crowd gathered to honor Freddie Gray. The 25-year-old died 15 days after he was arrested on a weapons charge. His death from a severe spinal cord injury sparked widespread outrage toward the Baltimore Police Department. His death in custody is the latest in a string of high profile deaths involving African-Americans and law enforcement. Many have demanded answers about what happened to Gray, and his funeral drew civil rights leaders, politicians, and relatives of others who died in police custody.

I have been a chef since I was 14 years old. In 2007, I started a food charity called Food Policy Action. This happened after I met a girl who was searching through trash for food to eat. Since then, I have worked on issues like hunger and factory farms. I did this with help from others, including an animation called "The Meatrix" from 2003. That video showed the health and environmental risks of factory farming.

Dan Swangard is a doctor who has seen many people die in hospitals. He has watched patients hooked to morphine drips struggle with anxiety as they passed away. He has also seen families stand by helplessly for weeks or months as their loved ones died.

Recently, Swangard’s thoughts about death have become personal. In 2013, he was diagnosed with a rare form of metastatic cancer. Surgeons removed parts of his pancreas and liver, as well as his spleen and gallbladder to treat the disease. The surgery was successful, but Swangard, 48, knows there is a strong chance the cancer will return.

CNN reports that Saudi special forces helped Yemeni fighters fight the Houthis and their allies in Aden. The special forces were on the ground in noncombat roles, coordinating and guiding the battle. They also helped parachute in weapons and communications equipment.

Following heavy Saudi airstrikes, Houthi rebels withdrew from the presidential palace and other key parts of the southern port city of Aden. This withdrawal signaled a reversal from rebel gains the previous day, when Houthi forces had seized the presidential palace.

A Detroit mother was arrested last month after police found two bodies in a freezer. Wayne County prosecutor Kym Worthy charged Mitchelle Angela Blair with murder and torture this week. Police Chief James Craig said a bailiff found the bodies during a court-ordered eviction on March 24. The medical examiner said the 13-year-old daughter, Stoni, died from blunt trauma, and the 9-year-old son, Stephen, died from blunt trauma and thermal injuries.

Miami (CNN) - World heavyweight boxing champion Wladimir Klitschko has a big fight coming up on April 25 against Bryant Jennings in New York. However, his mind is mostly on the crisis in Ukraine.

Speing to CNN from his Miami training camp, Klitschko said he is shocked and upset by the war between Ukraine and Russia. He said his country did not start the fight.

"My country is unfortunately suffering in the war with Russia -- not that Ukraine tried to give any aggression to any other nation, in this particular case Russia, unfortunately it's the other way around," Klitschko told CNN.

Michael Keaton hosted "Saturday Night Live" for the third time this weekend. He paid a small tribute to his famous roles as Beetlejuice and Batman. Keaton started hosting the show in 1982. He joked that he has a 31-year-old baby and a 28-year-old girlfriend. Fans wanted him to dress up as his famous characters, but he only made a few jokes about them.

Just over a month ago, a jury found Kamron Taylor guilty of murder. Early Wednesday morning, Taylor was in an Illinois jail. He hid in his cell and then ran out. He beat up a correctional officer, put on the guard's uniform, and took the keys. Taylor then walked out of the jail and into the officer's brown 2012 Chevrolet Equinox SUV. The 23-year-old, who was set to be sentenced in May, is now missing. The SUV was found around 8:30 a.m.

A New York City detective has been suspended after police say he stole $3,000 from a store. The detective was at the Yemen Deli and Grocery store in Brooklyn last Friday. He was caught on camera putting cash into a bag. The detectives had gone to the store to arrest two employees for selling loose cigarettes. The store manager, Ali Abdullah, noticed the money was missing from a box. He checked the cameras and could not believe what he saw.

London (CNN) A safe deposit company in London was broken into over the holiday weekend. Thieves used heavy cutting equipment and ropes to get into the 60-year-old vault. They spent possibly up to four days rumling through boxes, making this a nightmare for safe deposit box holders and a dream for movie directors. The thomers are reported to have gotten away with hundreds of thousands of pounds worth of gems and cash. One former police official guessed the total could be as high as 200 million pounds, or $300 million.

As South Africa remembers the 1994 elections on April 27, deadly attacks against African migrants have returned. Social outrage, shown by the #WeAreAfrica hashtag, highlights the need for unity. These attacks show that the country's dream of a non-racial society, where everyone lives with dignity, has failed.

In 1989, Ayatollah Khomeini said he was "drinking poison" when he agreed to a ceasefire that ended the eight-year war with Iraq. The war had helped define the Islamic Republic, which Khomeini had founded a year before Saddam Hussein invaded Iran. Khomeini encouraged both his supporters and opponents to fight the enemy. He dragged out the war for eight years, despite Saddam's willingness to accept a ceasefire, and thus stabilized the foundations of the Islamic Republic. By the time he ended the war, the economy was in shambles, and there was no sign of his die-hard volunteers.

CNN reports that the concept of sustainable development exists because raw capitalism has become too powerful. Global capitalism acts like a massive engine that doubles the world economy every generation. However, on a finite Earth with a billion new people added every 15 years, this engine is now attacking the physical foundations of life and the social systems that make life pleasant. Sustainable development is presented as a way out of this growing crisis. The reality is that raw capitalism is the economics of greed.

The United States has benefited greatly from being a leader in space travel. U.S. access to space has helped the country's national security, defense, and economy. The military relies on space-based capabilities like intelligence, GPS, and communications satellites to confront conflicts, fight terrorism, and handle worldwide threats. Unfortunately, as global threats increase and the need for secure space access grows, the U.S. is in a troubling reality: it is too reliant on Russian technology to meet its national security obligations.

On the one-year anniversary of the schoolgirls' abduction in Nigeria, Malala Yousafzai wrote an open letter to the missing students. The 17-year-old Nobel Peace Prize winner, who survived an attack by the Taliban in Pakistan, wrote that she was a target too because she wanted to go to school. In the letter, she asked the Nigerian government and the world to do more to rescue the girls. Nigeria had recently held an election.

CNN reports that South African soldiers were sent out Tuesday evening to help stop violent attacks against foreigners. The first place they went was the Johannesburg suburb of Jeppestown, where the violence started on Friday. Police raided a hostel in Jeppestown on Tuesday while soldiers guarded the area outside. The Minister of Defense, Nosiviwe Mapisa-Nqakula, said they are sending an unknown number of soldiers to places where police are too thin to stop the attacks. She said, "This move is not an attack on the police."

Eight Iranian border guards were killed in a fight with militants near the border with Pakistan, Iranian state media reported. Three of the militants were killed by Iranian forces in the fighting Monday in the southeastern town of Negur. The news agency said the militants crossed into the country from Pakistan. Iranian officials have reportedly asked Pakistani authorities to catch the surviving assailants.

TripAdvisor named Providenciales in the Turks and Caicos the world's top island. The island moved up from second place last year, pushing Ambergris Caye out of the top spot. Ambergris Caye had held the number one spot for two years, but dropped completely out of the top ten this year. TripAdvisor spokeswoman Julie Cassetina said it is hard to explain why winners change, based on traveler feedback.

At the Star Wars Celebration fan festival in Anaheim, California, details about the 2016 movie "Rogue One" were shared. Director Gareth Edwards showed a preview and confirmed the film will take place between "Episode III" and "Episode IV." The story follows a group of rebels on a dangerous mission to steal the Death Star plans. Felicity Jones plays a rebel soldier in the movie.

Tehran, Iran (CNN) -- A Persian proverb says, "A good year is determined by its spring." For many Iranians, the historic decision by Tehran and six world powers -- the United States, Britain, France, Germany, Russia and China -- to continue nuclear negotiations under a "joint comprehensive plan of action" is an indication that this year's Norouz, the Persian New Year that started on March 21, will be a superb one indeed. Although edgy hardliners may now try to play games and complain the preliminary agreement is not what they had hoped, for many people it shows excellent progress and that's what they want.

Ferguson, Missouri (CNN) -- Two African-American candidates, Ella Jones and Wesley Bell, were elected to the Ferguson City Council on Tuesday. This means three of the six council members are now black.

Elections opened at 6 a.m. on Tuesday. Traditionally, very few people vote in these municipal elections. However, today was different. This was the first city election since a white police officer shot and killed an unarmed black teenager named Michael Brown last August.

The skies grew ominous and the radio crackled with warnings of flash floods. Amid the rain, people went to the polls.

An Israeli man was killed and a woman was hurt in a suspected terror attack near Hebrew University in Jerusalem on Wednesday night. Police say a 37-year-old Arab driver from East Jerusalem hit two people waiting at a bus stop in the French Hill section of the city. One of the victims, named as Shalom Yohai Cherki, 26, died at the hospital. A 20-year-old woman is still in serious condition. The driver has been arrested and is being investigated by the General Security Services.

A collection of art owned by the late actress Lauren Bacall was sold at an auction in New York on March 31. The collection includes works by major 20th-century artists. It had been displayed in Hong Kong, Paris, London, and Los Angeles before the sale. Bacall, who died in 2014 at age 89, became famous in 1944 with the film "To Have and Have Not." She also met her husband, Humphrey Bogart, in that film. George Clooney honored her at the 2015 Golden Globes.

Kiev, Ukraine (CNN)
The question that is worrying the leaders in Kiev is this: Who might be killing allies of Ukraine's ousted President Viktor Yanukovych?

The idea that this is happening is not new. But it became important again this week with two high-profile shooting deaths in the Ukrainian capital -- one of a former member of parliament with ties to Yanukovych, the other of a Ukrainian journalist known for his pro-Russian views.

Oleg Kalashinkov, the former member of parliament, was shot and killed shortly after 7 p.m. Wednesday at the entrance to his apartment block.

CNN) Chile will soon recognize civil unions for same-sex couples. President Michelle Bachelet signed a new law on Monday that allows these unions. "This is a concrete step in the drive to end the difference between homosexual and heterosexual couples," Bachelet said. The law will take effect in six months. It gives legal rights to couples living together, whether they are same-sex or a man and a woman. The government estimates around 2 million people will benefit from this change.

The next time you fly to Florida to visit Grandma, or take the kids to see the " talking mouse," or go to South Beach for sun and fun, look out your window. Before you land, think about the huge swamp below.

The Everglades is a place that shows both the bad and the good parts of people. When planes land in Miami or Orlando, the ground looks like a wet, wild place full of things that can hurt you: snakes, scorpions, rats, roaches, gators, and mosquitoes. A researcher once caught 365,000 bloodthirsty bugs in a single trap in a single night.

CNN reports that ISIS militants took control of Yarmouk, a Palestinian refugee camp near Damascus, after defeating other militia groups there. The group stormed the area, flooding the streets. Residents who have been besieged and bombed by Syrian forces for over two years woke up to this terrifying new reality. One resident, who asked not to be named, told CNN that ISIS militants "slaughtered" people in the streets, including catching and killing three people in front of others. The Islamic State now controls almost all of the camp.

China's government has long blocked its citizens from reading Western news or other content it disapproves of using the "Great Firewall." A study published Friday says they have gone further. They have developed a new tool called the "Great Cannon" and have attacked servers outside China's borders, including in the United States. The study's authors say this visible and handy attack will likely draw anger from the international community, and Beijing may have counted on that.

A German official said investigators still do not know why co-pilot Andreas Lubitz crashed Germanwings Flight 9525. However, the official said Lubitz had suicidal thoughts before he became a pilot. Investigators have not found any notes or conversations where he explained his motives. Medical records show he was suicidal and saw a therapist before he ever got his pilot's license.

The leader of Yemen's Houthi rebels said on Sunday that his group would not give up. This came after a Saudi official claimed that weeks of airstrikes had weakened the rebels. In a TV address, the rebel leader Abdul-Malik al-Houthi said, "Our fighters will not leave the main cities or the government institutions. Anyone who thinks we will surrender is dreaming."

His comments followed more than three weeks of Saudi-led airstrikes. The goal of the bombing campaign was to push the Houthis back. The Houthis had surged into the capital of Sanaa in January and ousted President Abdu Rabu Mansour Hadi from power.

On April 19, 1995, Timothy McVeigh drove a truck filled with a bomb in front of the Murh Federal Building in Oklahoma City. The explosion killed 168 people and injured hundreds more. It remains the worst act of domestic terrorism in U.S. history.

The attack shocked the country. While the death toll was huge, the real surprise was that Americans had turned on their own government.

If you care deeply about something, you might protest, make a sign, or join a demonstration. How long could you keep going, in the face of indifference and inaction?

When more than 200 Nigerian girls were kidnapped from their school a year ago by Boko Haram militants, millions of people around the world joined a social media campaign to plead for their safe return. Charles Alasholuyi was one of those people -- from celebrities to world leaders -- voicing their anger via #BringBackOurGirls, one of the top Twitter hashtags of 2014, used in more than four million tweets. But as weeks turned into months, there was still no sign of the missing girls. The spotlight on the campaign faded.

Barney Frank, a retired congressman, recently appeared in Chicago. He entertained a sold-out crowd at the Center on Halsted by sharing stories from his 45-year career in public service. Frank was the first member of Congress to marry someone of the same-sex while in office. He also had strong words for politicians who are closeted and vote against LGBT rights. When a young man asked about a California ballot proposal that would legalize killing gay people, Frank said he was not aware of the measure but told the young man not to worry about "c crazy people."

CNN reports that a brutal attack on Garissa University College in Kenya left nearly 150 people dead, including students, and dozens more wounded. Gunmen attacked the campus early Thursday while morning prayers were happening, shooting randomly and taking hostages before being killed by security forces. The U.S. Embassy in Nairobi said Al-Shabaab militants claimed responsibility. The attack comes just months after Al-Shabaab militants murdered non-Muslim workers in a Kenyan quarry. The terrorist group has been behind numerous attacks in the region. It has also recruited some Americans, particularly from the Somali-American community in Minnesota.

Students at the University of Cape Town in South Africa have removed a statue of a British colonialist named Cecil Rhodes. The students had protested for weeks, saying on social media that his legacy was racist. The university agreed to remove the statue to keep it safe while they decide what to do with it in the future.

Syria is a very dangerous place. A group fighting the government says the number of people who have died has doubled in the last year. Since the civil war started, 310,000 people have been killed, according to the Syrian Observatory for Human Rights. A year ago, the number was 162,402. Before that, the United Nations said 70,000 people had died.

The United Nations also says that violence has hurt more than half of all Syrians. They are very poor and need help to survive. The U.N. says food rations have been cut because people have not donated enough money.

CNN reports that Ailina Tsarnaeva went into Manhattan Criminal Court quietly, but prosecutors say she was not shy about threatening a rival. According to a criminal complaint, Tsarnaeva called a woman this summer and threatened her, saying, "Leave my man alone." She also warned, "Stop looking for him. ... I know people that can put a bomb where you live." Prosecutors did not see this as a joke and charged Tsarnaeva with aggravated harassment, a charge she denies. Last December, Tsarnaeva and her lawyer refused to talk about the case. Tsarnaeva is the sister of Dzhokhar and Tamerlan Tsarnaev.

A Gaza police official said on Thursday that police took a door with a drawing by the artist Banksy. The owner, Rabea Darduna, said he sold the door for $175 because he did not know it was very valuable. His home was destroyed last summer, and he says the door was all he had left. The police are keeping the door until a court date.

A Saudi-led coalition is attacking Houthi rebels in Yemen. The coalition says it is gaining control, but locals are fleeing, and many people have been killed. Five days after the first airstrikes, the coalition has destroyed Houthi air defenses and those of President Ali Abdullah Saley. Most air bases and strips are unusable. Saudi Arabia's navy controls all Yemeni ports, only letting closely watched non-military medical goods pass through the blockade.

Holland manager Guus Hiddink was very angry about his fans booing Spain's Andres Iniesta during the 2-0 victory on Tuesday night. He called the fans a 'disgrace'. Spain coach Vicente del Bosque played with an experimental side, and Iniesta came into the game in the 76th minute. The home fans jeered and booed him. Stefan de Vrij and Davy Klaassen scored first-half goals for Holland. Spain midfielder Andres Iniesta controlled the ball during his side's 2-0 defeat by Holland on Tuesday night.

Scotland will find out on May 21 if their game against Georgia in September will be played with no fans in the stadium. UEFA has started an investigation against the Georgian Football Federation because fans ran onto the field twice during Sunday's 2-0 loss to Germany in Tbilisi. UEFA is also looking at charges that fans set off fireworks, and safety breaches like blocked stairs, locked gates, and a lack of body searches by staff at the Boris Paichadze Stadium. A fan ran onto the pitch during Georgia's 2-0 defeat by Germany on Sunday in Tbilisi.

Football agents were unsure about their future on Wednesday. Starting April 1, anyone can become a football agent by paying £500 for a one-year registration. The FA will then charge £250 every year to renew the license. People who were already licensed are exempt from these new rules. The FA was supposed to have a website link for agents to register, but it was not ready by 1pm. One man, Mel Stein, believes these new rules will cause chaos. These changes started because FIFA stopped governing agents.

CSKA Sofia's Latvian goalkeeper Maksims Uvarenko has not been paid for three months. He has had to ask his parents to send him money to pay his rent. Despite the financial problems, Uvarenko, who joined the Bulgarian club on an 18-month contract in January, has been impressed by the 'unique' fans and their passionate support. He told local media that the lack of money is the biggest problem he has faced at the club, and that he still has not received any salary.

David Moore, 25, got very angry while driving. He had just left his home and immediately found himself stuck in heavy traffic next to Rafal Cegielka, 45. Rafal was picking up his child from St John's Primary School in Burnley, Lancashire. Moore then punched the father and smashed his car with a hockey stick while children watched. This happened because Moore was having a "bad day" and was seeing things that weren't there.

Spain lost 2-0 to Holland on Tuesday. This loss reminded people of their bad performance in the 2014 World Cup. However, coach Vicente del Bosque is not worried about losing three friendly games in straight. Gerard Pique insists this. Holland, whose 5-1 drubbing of Spain in the group stage in Brazil last year marked the end of the Iberian nation's six-year domination of the world game, scored two early goals at the Amsterdam Arena and held on against some determined Spain pressure in the second half for a 2-0 success.

A New York City mother and her daughter have fled to Germany during a custody battle, police say. Ulrike Berger, 44, is not allowed to leave the country with her seven-year-old daughter Kaia. However, on March 22, a day after the little girl was dropped off for a weekend visit, they are believed to have boarded a plane to Europe.

Manhunt: Police are searching for Ulrike Berger, 44, and her seven-year-old daughter Kaia. It is believed the pair boarded a plane from New York to Germany on March 22, violating a custody court order. Police say the pair were last seen at Berger's home in Boerun Hill, Brooklyn, at 10am on March 21, when Ka

A huge fire ripped through dry heathland near the south coast. The fire looked like a disaster movie. It burned an area the size of 100 football pitches. The fire happened after days of storms that felled trees and shut roads.

The fire started in Dorset. The area was very dry because it was on a hill and rain had run off. Fire investigators say the fire was started on purpose. Three areas of heath were destroyed. The sizes were half a hectare, one hectare, and 70 hectares.

Last night, emergency services were very busy. They received about 600 calls every hour because people were drinking heavily. Parmedics were very busy, and in Cambridge, they set up a hospital to help people who were drunk.

In London, the ambulance service said they were getting over 600 calls at the peak time. This was more than three times the number of calls they usually get at night.

In Manchester, a man collapsed on the pavement next to an ambulance. Two people were walking past eating food. Also in Manchester, a man was slumped over in a doorway while two women walked by him celebrating the New Year.

Liverpool goalkeeper Simon Mignolet said his mental strength helped him recover after being dropped in December. Mignolet was left out of the team indefinitely by manager Brendan Rodgers following a poor run of form, but he returned to the side after Brad Jones got hurt. The 27-year-old Belgian said he tried to stay upbeat despite the disappointment. Mignolet told FourFourTwo: 'I was positive.'

Giant hailstones the size of plums crashed down over the South on Tuesday with residents rushing out to capture the freak weather. Twitter user Arke USA from Bryant, Arkansas, filmed the ice balls peppering his backyard and noisily plopping into the swimming pool. Footage shows the hailstones coming down at speed, with many cracking as they hit the ground. Despite it being around 80-degrees, the compacted lumps prove resilient to the heat taking a good while to melt. In a matter of seconds the patio is completely covered in snow-white pellets.
